newsitem.title: FRANCE: Hoechst to buy rest of Roussel for $3.5 billion.
newsitem.headline: Hoechst to buy rest of Roussel for $3.5 billion.

text.p: Germany's Hoechst AG Wednesday offered to buy the rest of French drug maker Roussel Uclaf for about $3.5 billion in a move to strengthen its hand on both sides of the Atlantic in the rapidly consolidating pharmaceutical industry.

Hoechst, which holds 56.5 percent of Roussel Uclaf, maker of the RU-486 abortion drug, said the move would help create a simpler structure for its Hoechst Marion Roussel unit formed last year with the $7.1 billion acquisition of Marion Merrell Dow in the United States. Hoechst Marion Roussel is the world's fourth largest drug maker.

The move marks another step away from the commodity chemicals business and into higher-profit drugs for Hoechst, Europe's biggest chemical company. Hoechst said Tuesday it would sell its speciality chemicals unit to Clariant AG of Switzerland to cope with stiff competition in the sector.

"This particular transaction is designed to maximize our opportunities in the pharmaceuticals area and come up with a Hoechst Marion Roussel operation which is globally integrated and which can therefore better face the competition," Hoechst Finance Director Klaus Schmieder told a news conference.
Industry analysts had been expecting Hoechst to bid for the rest of Roussel as a step toward an initial stock offering for Hoechst Marion Roussel.
But Schmieder said while Hoechst planned to issue its own stock on the New York Stock Exchange next year, any decision to float Hoechst Marion Roussel shares would depend on market conditions.

"As long as we feel that the stock price of Hoechst AG does not adequately reflect the value of the group, the listing of (Hoechst Marion Roussel) becomes an issue and we will make a decision going forward," he said.

Hoechst Marion Roussel had sales of about $8.6 billion last year and spent nearly $1.3 billion on research and development. It employs 40,500 people and has 3.6 percent of the world pharmaceutical market and 3.7 percent of the U.S. market, officials said.
The deal is one of the biggest announced this year on the Paris stock exchange and continues the worldwide consolidation that is reshaping the pharmaceutical industry.

It would boost Hoechst's strength in Germany, France and the United States, but the company would still rank behind Glaxo Wellcome Plc, Novartis, being formed by the merger of Swiss drug makers Ciba Geigy AG and Sandoz AG, and Merck & Co.
Analysts said the move put Hoechst in an even stronger position as a leading drug maker worldwide.

While the price was high, they said Hoechst could afford it since it was cutting about $2.6 billion in debt under the sale to Clariant, in which it would take up to a 45 percent stake in the merged operation.
Roussel, which had 1995 sales of about $3.2 billion and net profit of $195 million, also makes veterinary products and chemicals for agriculture and other markets. It has about 14,000 employees.
Hoechst, with about $33.6 billion in sales and $1.1 billion in profits last year, makes a wide range of drugs and chemicals and employs about 166,000 people.
Hoechst is offering 1,530 francs ($294) per Roussel common share and 1,330 francs ($256) for each preferred share, amounting to 18.1 billion francs ($3.5 billion), Hoechst said.
That represents a 12 percent premium on the average price of the common stock over the previous month and 19 percent over the average over the previous three months, Hoechst said.
